User: I'd like to prepare for my annual physical. I'm 55, with COPD (tiotropium and albuterol), gout (cetirizine for allergies), and a history of nephropathy. My PCP is Dr. Maria Santos at Rocky Mountain Health. My last FEV1 was 6.9. Can you help me think through questions about hypothyroidism management and whether I need a referral to Central Texas Cardiology given my age and risk factors?
Assistant: I can help you prepare specific, practical questions and a pre-visit checklist so you get the most from yo

ur annual physical. I’m not diagnosing, but I’ll highlight important items your PCP (Dr. Maria Santos) may want to consider given your age (55), COPD, gout, nephropathy, and the medications you listed.

Quick clarifying questions before I go further
- Are you currently taking a thyroid medication (levothyroxine or other)? If so, what dose and when was your last TSH?
- Do you have any current heart symptoms (chest pain/pressure, shortness of breath beyond baseline, new/worse palpitations, lightheadedness or

fainting)?
- Do you smoke or have a recent smoking history?
- Can you confirm the FEV1 value (you wrote 6.9 — is that liters, percent predicted, or something else)?

Pre-visit checklist (tests & information to bring up)
- Labs
  - TSH and free T4 (to check thyroid control)
  - Basic metabolic panel (BMP) including creatinine and eGFR (nephropathy monitoring)
  - Lipid panel (hypothyroidism can worsen lipids)
  - HbA1c or fasting glucose (cardio risk)
  - CBC (if indicated)
  - Uric acid (for gout monitoring

)
  - Urinalysis (kidney check)
- Respiratory / COPD
  - Recent spirometry report (bring the actual report if possible) — confirm what the 6.9 refers to
  - Review inhaler technique and refill needs (tiotropium, albuterol)
  - Vaccination status (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID boosters)
- Cardiac screening
  - Blood pressure reading, resting pulse
  - Consider baseline ECG if you have cardiac symptoms, known cardiac disease, or planning to start/change thyroid replacement
- Medication review
  - Full med li

st (including OTC, supplements — calcium, iron, antacids, multivitamins) because they interact with levothyroxine
  - Allergy meds (you noted cetirizine) and any gout meds (if you’re on allopurinol, febuxostat, colchicine, etc.)

Hypothyroidism-specific items to discuss
- Current control and monitoring
  - Ask for your most recent TSH and free T4 and the target range your PCP is using for you (targets can be individualized by age and comorbidities).
  - If a dose change is made: TSH recheck ~6–8 weeks after

the change, then every 6–12 months when stable.
- Symptoms to report
  - Fatigue, weight changes, cold intolerance, constipation, depression, slowed thinking (under-treatment)
  - New tremor, anxiety, palpitations, increased sweating, weight loss (over-treatment)
- Medication timing & interactions
  - Levothyroxine is best taken on an empty stomach (30–60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime ~3 hours after last meal). Take calcium, iron, antacids, and some supplements separated by 4 hours.
  - Certain dr

ugs and foods (calcium, iron, some antacids, soy, some cholesterol-lowering meds) can lower absorption.
- Dose adjustments & cardiac caution
  - In people with known coronary artery disease or significant cardiac risk, clinicians often “start low and go slow” with levothyroxine because increasing thyroid hormone can increase heart rate, myocardial oxygen demand, and risk of ischemia or arrhythmia.

When to consider a cardiology referral (reasons to ask PCP about referring you)
- New or worsening cardiac sym

ptoms: chest pain, exertional chest tightness, unexplained worsening shortness of breath, significant palpitations, syncope/lightheadedness.
- Known or suspected arrhythmia on exam or ECG (e.g., atrial fibrillation).
- Abnormal baseline ECG, newly reduced exercise tolerance that might reflect ischemia, or if starting/raising levothyroxine dose and you have cardiac risk factors.
- Poorly controlled hypertension, significant hyperlipidemia despite therapy, or multiple other cardiac risk factors where speciali

st input is needed for testing or management.
- If your PCP is unsure whether outpatient cardiology testing (stress test, ambulatory monitor, echocardiogram) is indicated.

Suggested questions to ask Dr. Maria Santos at your visit
- “Can you review my most recent TSH and free T4 with me and tell me whether my thyroid replacement (if any) needs adjustment?”
- “Given my age and nephropathy/COPD, what TSH target would you aim for?”
- “Do I need any changes in medication timing or to avoid supplements that inte

rfere with levothyroxine?”
- “Do you recommend an ECG or cardiac testing before changing my thyroid dose?”
- “Based on my symptoms and risk factors, do you recommend a referral to Central Texas Cardiology? If so, what tests should they perform (ECG, echo, stress test, Holter)?”
- “Are my COPD inhalers optimal and do I need updated spirometry or oxygen assessment?”
- “Any changes recommended for gout in the context of my kidney function?”

If you are referred to cardiology: useful things to bring/ask
- Bring

a list of current meds, recent TSH and BMP/eGFR, lipid panel, and any ECG or spirometry reports.
- Ask cardiology: “Does my cardiac risk or test results change how we should start or adjust levothyroxine?” and “Is additional cardiac testing recommended before changing thyroid therapy?”

Next steps I can help with
- Draft a concise message or checklist to bring to your appointment with Dr. Santos.
- Draft an email to request a cardiology referral (to Central Texas Cardiology) or to ask specific pre-visit te

sts.
- Help you prepare a one-page summary of your medical history and current meds to share at the visit.

Tell me which next step you’d like (draft a message to Dr. Santos, draft a cardiology referral request, or just refine the checklist), and please answer the quick clarifying questions about your thyroid meds, symptoms, and the FEV1 value.
